body.text: In Canada's SR&ED program, overhead and other expenditures are claimed only by claimants using the Traditional Method, on Line 360 of Form T661, and must be both directly related and incremental to SR&ED under the Income Tax Regulations. Claimants electing the Proxy Method instead earn credits on a prescribed proxy amount equal to 55% of the salary base.

This report provides a comprehensive legal, technical, and financial audit of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program and provincial and territorial research and development (R&D) tax credit regimes in Canada as of November 20261.

Canada's R&D tax landscape has undergone its most significant structural expansion in over a decade following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 20262. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the enacted legislation doubles the federal annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3.0 million to $6.0 million (superseding the interim $4.5 million proposal from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), raising the maximum annual enhanced refundable federal credit from $1.05 million to $2.10 million2. Furthermore, Bill C-15 expands the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extends access to the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure (which Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] may also elect to use), and restores the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 20241. Operationally, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval Process that halves post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days9.

Concurrently, major structural reforms have reshaped both federal commercialization policy and provincial R&D regimes. According to tax advisory analysis of Federal Budget 2026 (tabled on November 5, 2026, by Minister of Finance François-Philippe Champagne), the federal government has proposed to expand SR&ED eligibility—effective for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026—to cover post-R&D regulatory testing, validation, certification, and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs linked to an eligible SR&ED project, alongside a permanent Productivity Mega Deduction providing 100% first-year write-offs for most depreciable property acquired on or after September 15, 20264. At the provincial level, Quebec replaced eight legacy R&D and design tax credits with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, providing a fully refundable 30% credit on the first $1.0 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold (and 20% on the excess) regardless of company size8. British Columbia expressly harmonized with the federal $6.0 million expenditure limit, ECPC expansion, and capital expenditure restoration while making its 10% credit permanent in B.C. Budget 2026, and Saskatchewan doubled its refundable CCPC threshold from $1.0 million to $2.0 million for expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 20243. Conversely, Ontario ($3.0 million OITC limit) and Alberta ($4.0 million Innovation Employment Grant limit) have retained their independent expenditure caps3.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Primary Statutory Authorities: The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR)14. The program delivers two distinct, mutually reinforcing statutory incentives to taxpayers carrying on business in Canada18.

First, under Section 37 of the ITA, the SR&ED Expenditure Deduction Pool allows a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to pool allowable current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year, deduct all or any portion of the pool against net business income in the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years18. Second, under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA, the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) generates a federal tax credit equal to a prescribed percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of the claimant's "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year1. Depending on the legal status of the claimant and the nature of the expenditure, unused ITCs may reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable, be refunded in cash under Section 127.1, or be carried back three taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years under subsection 127(5)1.

body.text: 1.2 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act7. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and encompasses three core categories of foundational work, one category of derivative support work, and seven explicit statutory exclusions7.
A. Core Categories of Eligible SR&ED Work
The definition in subsection 248(1) establishes three foundational categories of research and development33:

items: Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view29.
Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view29.

Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto29. Experimental development is the most frequently claimed category in Canadian industrial and commercial SR&ED claims33. Crucially, the statute expressly protects incremental improvements, provided the work is undertaken to resolve a genuine technological uncertainty and achieve a technological advancement rather than applying routine engineering7.

body.text: B. Eligible Support Work

In addition to the three core categories, subsection 248(1) includes support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research29. Support work does not qualify as SR&ED on a standalone basis28. To be eligible, the work must satisfy a dual nexus test: it must be (1) commensurate with the needs, and (2) directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer29.
C. Statutory Exclusions from SR&ED (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))
Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes work with respect to seven enumerated activities in paragraphs (e) to (k) from the definition of SR&ED29:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion29;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes29;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities29;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas29;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process29;
Paragraph (j): Style changes29; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection29.

body.text: As clarified in the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives (published August 13, 2021, and updated July 5, 2022), the fundamental criterion distinguishing eligible support work (such as data collection or testing) from excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) (such as routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose29. If testing or data collection is carried out specifically to test a hypothesis and resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty within an active SR&ED project, it qualifies as eligible support work29. Conversely, if the same physical testing protocol is performed to verify commercial compliance or routine quality assurance, it is statutorily excluded29.
1.3 Evolution of CRA Administrative Eligibility Guidance: From IC 86-4R3 to the "Why and How" Framework
The administrative interpretation of subsection 248(1) has evolved through four distinct eras, while the underlying statutory text of subsection 248(1) has remained constant since 199232.

Prior to 1985, Revenue Canada relied on Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 to assess whether work met the regulatory definition of research and development32. Following taxpayer feedback that IT-439 was insufficient, the Department of Finance announced in the May 1985 Budget Papers that it would introduce the term "experimental development" to confirm that projects involving only routine engineering or routine development were excluded32. On March 4, 1986, the Department of Finance confirmed that eligible R&D must embody scientific or technological advancement, involve scientific or technological uncertainty, and be carried out in a systematic and organized fashion32. Revenue Canada and industry leaders subsequently developed Information Circular IC 86-4 in 1986 (culminating in IC 86-4R3 in 1994), which formalized the three foundational criteria—scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content—that were later adopted by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998)7.

Following Northwest Hydraulic, the CRA consolidated its administrative framework into the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (first published in 2012, revised in 2015, and archived in August 2021), which evaluated claims using five sequential questions derived directly from Chief Justice Bowman's jurisprudence32. In August 2021, as part of a program modernization initiative launched in 2020, the CRA replaced the 2012/2015 policy with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives32. The 2021 Guidelines consolidated the five questions into two overarching requirements derived from subsection 248(1)29:

The first requirement is the "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty). Work must be conducted for the purpose of advancing scientific knowledge or achieving a technological advancement by generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories or prediction models) rather than purely factual measurements29. New knowledge is required when there is scientific or technological uncertainty—defined as an insufficiency or gap in publicly available and internal business scientific or technological knowledge, indicated by inapplicable existing design methods, interlocking constraints, excessive variables or unknowns, evolving problem dynamics, or parameters outside normal operating ranges29. Attempting to circumvent an uncertainty via standard workarounds, or merely acquiring existing knowledge through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert consultants, or purchasing proprietary know-how, does not satisfy the "Why" requirement29. Whether the project ultimately succeeds or fails in achieving its objectives is irrelevant; eligibility depends strictly on the purpose of the work at the time it is undertaken33.

The second requirement is the "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search). Work must be carried out through a systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis29. This requires four methodical steps: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation; (2) testing that idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses); (3) developing logical conclusions based on the experimental results or findings; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence that is generated as the work progresses29. As the Federal Court of Appeal expressly held in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, the CRA's 2021 "Why" and "How" guidelines are an administrative restatement that is consistent with—and does not eliminate or relax—the binding five-part common-law test established in Northwest Hydraulic and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 8842.
1.4 The 2025–2026 Legislative Reforms: Bill C-15 (Enacted) and Federal Budget 2026 (Proposed)
A. Enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1)

Following initial consultations in 2024, the Department of Finance Canada announced sweeping enhancements to the SR&ED program in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) and expanded them further in Budget 2025 (presented November 4, 2025, by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne)1. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, enacting these measures into law retroactive to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (and, for capital property and lease costs, property acquired or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024)2.

To align with Bill C-15, the CRA issued updated prescribed forms and administrative policies throughout 2026, including revised Form T661 (May 15, 2026), Form T1145 (May 15, 2026), Form T1146 (May 15, 2026), Schedule T2SCH31 (May 22, 2026), Schedule T2SCH49 (May 29, 2026), the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), the Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (May 22, 2026), the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8 / June 22, 2026), the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), and the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026)1.
B. Federal Budget 2026 Proposals (Tabled November 5, 2026)

According to tax advisory analysis of Federal Budget 2026 (tabled on November 5, 2026, by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne), the federal government has proposed a second wave of innovation and capital investment incentives designed to bridge the gap between laboratory R&D and commercial deployment4.

First, Budget 2026 proposes to expand SR&ED eligibility beyond prototyping into commercialization testing, certification, and IP protection4. Historically, federal SR&ED eligibility stopped once technological uncertainty was resolved ("at the lab door")4. Budget 2026 allocates $930 million over five years (and $235 million annually thereafter) to expand SR&ED eligible expenditures—applying to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026—to include two new post-R&D categories, provided the underlying product or process originated from an eligible SR&ED project4:

items: Testing and Regulatory Certification: Covers tests, technological validations, and studies required to obtain initial approval or certification for a new product or process, claimable across standard SR&ED categories (salaries, materials, contracts, overhead, and machinery/equipment)4. Re-certification due to supplier changes, annual surveillance audits, and routine compliance testing are excluded4.

Intellectual Property Protection and Maintenance: Covers registration and maintenance costs for patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software protected under Canadian law or foreign equivalents4. While administrative filing and maintenance fees paid to foreign IP offices qualify, supporting application activities (such as preparation) qualify only if conducted in Canada; IP litigation and enforcement costs are excluded4. Once the legislation receives Royal Assent, corporations will also no longer be required to file a certified directors' resolution with elections for SR&ED expenditure transfers4.

body.text: Second, Budget 2026 confirms the proposed permanent Productivity Mega Deduction (100% first-year write-off), originally announced on September 15, 20264. Budgeted at $36 billion over five years, this proposed permanent measure would allow businesses to deduct up to 100% of the cost of most depreciable property acquired on or after September 15, 2026, in the first taxation year the asset becomes available for use, covering over 65% of business investments and lowering Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new investment from 13% to 6.4%4. For shared-use equipment (used >50% to <90% in SR&ED) and commercial production equipment, this would provide an immediate 100% year-one Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) write-off alongside any applicable SR&ED ITCs (note that the Mega Deduction would have to be claimed in the first year the asset becomes available for use, whereas standard Section 37 SR&ED pool deductions can be carried forward indefinitely)4.
2. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Expenditure Limits, Refundability, and Carryovers
2.1 The Two-Tier Federal ITC Structure: 35% Enhanced Rate vs. 15% Basic Rate
Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act, federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits are calculated under a two-tier rate regime1.

The Enhanced ITC Rate (35%) is calculated as the 15% basic ITC rate under subsection 127(9) plus an additional 20% enhancement under subsection 127(10.1)1. Prior to December 16, 2024, the 35% enhanced rate was restricted exclusively to Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3.0 million1. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn the 35% enhanced rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to an expanded annual expenditure limit of $6.0 million1.

The Basic ITC Rate (15%) applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a CCPC or ECPC in excess of its available annual expenditure limit for the taxation year, as well as to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by other corporations (such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries and non-ECPC public corporations), individuals, trusts, and partners in a partnership1. Claimants must closely monitor CCPC status, which turns on corporate control rather than share ownership alone; a shareholder agreement or option that grants non-residents a right to acquire control can cause a corporation to lose CCPC status and forfeit the 35% enhanced rate4.
2.2 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Introduced for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the definition of an "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) in subsection 127(9) of the ITA extends the 35% enhanced refundable ITC (up to the $6.0 million expenditure limit) to domestic public innovators1. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory conditions8:

items: Canadian Residency: The corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year8;

Public Corporation Status: The corporation must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation)8; and

Absence of Non-Resident Control: The corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons (even if all shares owned by non-residents were assumed to be owned by a single particular person, it would still not be controlled by that person)8.

body.text: In addition, Canadian-resident corporations all or substantially all (90% or more) of whose shares are owned by one or more ECPCs also qualify10. If an ECPC is a member of a corporate group that prepares consolidated financial statements, the $6.0 million expenditure limit must be shared and allocated among all members of the consolidated group pursuant to subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.63) of the ITA1.
2.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue Election

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6.0 million maximum expenditure limit is subject to a straight-line reduction (phase-out) between $15.0 million and $75.0 million under one of two statutory methodologies1.
A. Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out Method (Default for CCPCs — Subsections 127(10.2) & 127(10.21))

For a CCPC (and its associated corporations across Canada), the annual expenditure limit is reduced based on the taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning of Part I.3 of the ITA, as referenced in CRA bulletin IT-532) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for the immediately preceding taxation year1. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 limit began decreasing once prior-year associated taxable capital reached $10,000,000 and was reduced to nil at $50,000,000 (a reduction of $0.075 of expenditure limit for every $1.00 of taxable capital above $10,000,000)1. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 limit begins decreasing once prior-year associated taxable capital reaches $15,000,000 and is eliminated completely at $75,000,000 (a reduction of $0.10 of expenditure limit for every $1.00 of taxable capital above $15,000,000)1: Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year associated taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

While prior-year federal taxable income does not reduce the $6.0 million federal expenditure limit itself, prior-year taxable income (specifically whether it exceeds the qualifying income limit of $500,000) still determines whether a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" eligible for 40% refundability on basic 15% ITCs earned above the expenditure limit1.
B. Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out Method (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs — Subsections 127(10.31), 127(10.32) & 127(10.6))

Under subsection 127(10.6) of the ITA, the expenditure limit for an ECPC is phased out on a straight-line basis based on its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, as reflected in the financial statements of the corporation or the consolidated financial statements of its consolidated group1. If the three-year average annual gross revenue is $15,000,000 or less, the expenditure limit is the full $6,000,0008. If the three-year average annual gross revenue is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the $6,000,000 limit is reduced on a straight-line basis ($0.10 per $1.00 of average revenue above $15,000,000) and becomes nil ($0) once three-year average annual gross revenue reaches $75,000,0008: Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if three-year average annual revenue is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average exceeds $15,000,000.

If an entity leaves or joins a consolidated ECPC group during the year, the average annual revenue used is that of the consolidated group as reflected in the consolidated financial statements for the year in question1.

Crucially, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) of the ITA, a CCPC (or, under subsection 127(10.32), an associated group of CCPCs) may elect on a prescribed form to calculate its expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure instead of the prior-year taxable capital structure1. This allows capital-intensive CCPCs with high balance-sheet taxable capital (over $15 million) but low or nil historical gross revenue to select the method that yields the highest expenditure limit10. When an associated group of CCPCs elects the revenue method, the calculation requires summing all amounts of average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for the preceding three fiscal years for each corporation that is a member of the group for the tax year in question, regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout that entire three-year period1.
C. Short Taxation Year Proration (Subsection 127(10.5))

If a CCPC or ECPC has a short taxation year (less than 51 weeks), its expenditure limit is prorated under paragraph 127(10.5)(b) (paragraph 127(10.64)(b) for ECPCs) by multiplying the expenditure limit otherwise determined by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 3651. For example, as illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, a corporation with a $3,000,000 allocated expenditure limit and a 184-day short taxation year from July 1 to December 31 has a prorated limit of $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) = $1,512,3281.

body.text: 2.5 Federal ITC Refundability Matrix by Claimant Classification

Under Section 127.1 (Refundable Investment Tax Credit) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), the percentage of unused current-year SR&ED ITCs that can be refunded in cash (after offsetting federal Part I tax payable) depends strictly on: (1) the legal classification of the claimant; (2) whether the expenditure is within or above the $6.0 million expenditure limit; and (3) whether the expenditure is of a current nature (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount) or a capital nature1.

Crucially, a refund percentage applies to the credit earned, rather than to the original spending8. Thus, a 40% refund rate on a 35% capital ITC yields an effective cash refund equal to 14.0% of the capital expenditure (35% × 40% = 14%), while the remaining 60% of the credit (21.0% of the expenditure) remains a non-refundable ITC available to offset Part I tax or be carried back 3 years / forward 20 years1. Similarly, a 40% refund rate on a 15% basic ITC yields an effective cash refund equal to 6.0% of the qualified expenditure (15% × 40% = 6%)8.
To classify corporate claimants accurately under Section 127.1, the ITA distinguishes four corporate categories1:

items: Qualifying Corporation (other than an Excluded Corporation): A CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (plus that of associated corporations, if applicable) was not more than its qualifying income limit for the current year (which begins at $500,000 and phases out based on prior-year taxable capital)1.

CCPC that is Not a Qualifying Corporation (and Not an Excluded Corporation): A CCPC whose prior-year associated taxable income exceeded its qualifying income limit, but whose prior-year taxable capital (or 3-year average gross revenue if elected) is below $75 million so that it still retains an expenditure limit1.
Excluded Corporation: A CCPC that is classified as an excluded corporation under subsection 127.1(2) (which restricts refundability to 40% across both current and capital expenditures)1.
Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC): A Canadian-resident, exchange-listed public corporation not controlled by non-residents (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024)1.

body.text: Illustrative Federal Refund Calculation (Post-December 15, 2024 Rules)

Consider a Qualifying CCPC with prior-year taxable capital below the $15.0 million phase-out threshold and prior-year taxable income within the qualifying income limit that incurs $8,000,000 in qualified current SR&ED expenditures during its 2025/2026 taxation year1. On the first $6,000,000 (up to the Expenditure Limit), the CCPC earns the 35% enhanced rate ($6,000,000 × 35% = $2,100,000 ITC), which is 100% refundable on current expenditures, generating $2,100,000 in cash1. On the next $2,000,000 (in excess of the Expenditure Limit), the CCPC earns the 15% basic rate ($2,000,000 × 15% = $300,000 ITC), which for a Qualifying Corporation is 40% refundable, generating $300,000 × 40% = $120,000 in cash1. Total federal ITC earned is $2,400,000, of which $2,220,000 is paid out immediately as a cash refund (assuming nil Part I tax payable) and $180,000 ($300,000 minus $120,000) is retained as a non-refundable ITC carryforward1. By contrast, had the claimant been an ECPC or a Non-Qualifying CCPC, it would receive the same $2,100,000 cash refund on the first $6,000,000, but 0% refundability on the $300,000 basic ITC over the limit, leaving all $300,000 as a non-refundable carryforward1.
2.6 Carryforwards, Carrybacks, Pool Deductions, and Assignment Rules

Under subsection 127(5) of the ITA, any portion of an SR&ED ITC earned in a taxation year that is neither applied to reduce current-year Part I tax nor refunded under Section 127.1 may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the lesser of the unused current-year ITC and the Part I tax otherwise payable in that preceding year) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset future Part I federal income tax1. An ITC refund can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the underlying expenditure was incurred, and cannot be claimed in respect of repayments of assistance or contract payments8.

Under subsection 37(1), allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures added to the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures may be deducted in whole, in part, or not at all in the current taxation year (on Form T2SCH1), and any positive balance carries forward indefinitely to future taxation years20. However, three critical pool rules govern carryforwards and adjustments:

items: Prior-Year ITC Pool Reduction and Negative Pool Income Inclusion (Paragraph 12(1)(v)): Federal SR&ED ITCs applied against tax or refunded in cash in a preceding year reduce the claimant's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the current taxation year (reported on Line 435 of Form T661)19. If the reductions to the Section 37 pool exceed the additions and opening balance—resulting in a negative pool balance at the end of the taxation year—that negative balance must be included in net income for tax purposes in that year under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA, and the amount brought into income is added back to reset the subsequent year's opening pool balance to nil (zero)20.

Loss Restriction Event / Acquisition of Control (Subsection 37(6.1) & Paragraph 37(1)(h)): When control of a corporation is acquired (or a trust has a new majority-interest beneficiary), a loss restriction event occurs and the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool is reduced to nil20. Under subsection 37(6.1), pre-acquisition pool amounts can be reinstated and deducted in post-acquisition years only when the business to which the expenditure related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent that the corporation's income for the year (before any Section 37 deduction) is from that same business or a similar business20.

Partnership Pool Restriction (Paragraph 96(1)(e.1)): Unlike corporations or individuals, a partnership cannot carry forward an amount in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal year; the entire balance of the partnership's Section 37 pool at the end of its fiscal year must be fully deducted in calculating the partnership's net income for tax purposes for that year20.

body.text: Finally, with respect to assignments of refundable ITCs, while Canadian companies frequently utilize SR&ED financing loans to access capital prior to receiving their tax refund45, the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy confirms that although a corporation may make an assignment under subsections 220(6) and 220(7) of the ITA, such assignments are not binding on the CRA8. Under no circumstances will CRA refund cheques be made payable to an assignee; cheques are issued solely in the name of the claimant (though a claimant may attach a written request to its T2 return asking that a specific refund cheque be mailed to a "care of" [c/o] address)8.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methodologies, and Cost Rules
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method: Strategic Election and Mechanics

To calculate allowable SR&ED expenditures in Part 3 of Form T661 and qualified SR&ED expenditures in Part 4, a claimant must elect on Line 160 (Proxy Method) or Line 162 (Traditional Method) of Form T66119. The election is made annually for each taxation year and cannot be changed for that taxation year once the return/form is filed; if a claimant fails to select a method, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method by default46.

body.text: 3.2 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and the Overall Cap Formula

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations sets the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) at 55% of the salary base19. Historically, the PPA rate was 65% for 2012 and prior years and 60% for 2013, before being permanently set at 55% starting in 2014 (any secondary guide or forum referencing 65% reflects pre-2013 rates)8.
A. Exclusions from the Salary Base (Regulation 2900(9))

The "salary base" (calculated in Part 5, Section A of Form T661) begins with the eligible salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (and permissible foreign SR&ED wages), but subsection 2900(9) of the Regulations mandates excluding all of the following amounts for any employee, whether a specified employee or not19:

items: Taxable benefits under Section 6 of the ITA and stock option benefits under Section 7 of the ITA19;
Bonuses and remuneration based on profits19;
Unpaid remuneration from a prior taxation year paid in the current taxation year and deemed incurred under subsection 78(4) (Line 310 of Form T661)25; and
Employer's contributions / related benefits (such as employer portions of CPP, QPP, EI, or group insurance)25.

body.text: B. The Overall Cap on the PPA (Regulation 2900(6))

To ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed the total business expenditures made in the taxation year, subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA25: Overall Cap = A − B − C

In this statutory formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of specific statutory deductions claimed under Section 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, and bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on a business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), Section 37 (SR&ED expenditures deducted in the year), Sections 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts); and C is the total of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as rent)25. If a claimant carries on more than one business, the deductions from all businesses must be summed25. In practice, the Overall Cap does not restrict the PPA provided the business has deducted more than $55 of eligible non-SR&ED, non-building-rent, non-Section-20 expenses for each $100 of eligible salary included in the salary base25.
3.3 Salary or Wages: Directly Engaged, Specified Employees, Unpaid Wages, and Foreign Work

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), allowable employee remuneration is governed by strict statutory rules regarding employee duties, shareholder status, payment timing, and geography34.
A. "Directly Engaged" vs. "Undertakes, Supervises, or Supports"

Under the Proxy Method (and for hands-on staff under the Traditional Method), "directly engaged" captures hands-on work performing basic research, applied research, or experimental development, performing eligible support work directly in support of SR&ED, and first-line supervision—where managers or supervisors direct ongoing technical work or provide direct technical input34. Higher-level management and non-technological activities (such as strategic planning, corporate direction, clerical, payroll, accounting, legal, shipping, reception, or human resources) do not qualify as "directly engaged"34. Under subsection 2900(5) of the Regulations, if an employee spends all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of their employment time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be included; otherwise, only the portion that can reasonably be considered to relate to SR&ED qualifies25.

Under the Traditional Method, claimants may also claim on Line 360 (as overhead and other expenditures) the salaries or wages of non-technological administrative or clerical staff (HR, accounting, purchasing) and the employer's share of related benefits (CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, approved pension plans, and medical/dental/optical insurance) for hands-on SR&ED employees, provided those expenditures are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED19. Under both methods, stock option benefits (Section 7), extended vacation or sick leave in excess of normal annual entitlements, and retiring allowances are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages (though a retiring allowance may qualify as traditional overhead if directly related and incremental)34. Furthermore, where a non-cash taxable benefit is included in SR&ED wages, it must represent a reasonable estimate of actual costs not otherwise claimed as a business expense and must exclude any GST/HST or PST for which an input tax credit or rebate can be claimed (as GST/HST input tax credits are deemed to be government assistance under subsection 248(16))34.
B. Specified Employees: Definition and Dual Statutory Caps

A "specified employee" is an individual who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who holds, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of a related corporation34. Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions under subsection 37(9.3) of the ITA and subsections 2900(7) to 2900(10) of the Regulations24:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration: Bonuses, profit-sharing remuneration, and performance-based incentives paid to specified employees are completely excluded from both allowable SR&ED salary or wages and the proxy salary base25. (For non-specified employees, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are allowable SR&ED wages on Line 300, though excluded from the proxy salary base on Line 81219.)

The 75% Maximum Allocation Cap: The maximum portion of a specified employee's total eligible salary or wages (excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year) that can be claimed for SR&ED and included in the salary base is capped at 75%25.

The 2.5 × YMPE Ceiling: The total eligible SR&ED salary or wages and salary base inclusion for a specified employee cannot exceed 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the claimant's tax year ends, prorated by the number of days the claimant employed the individual in the tax year (with no proration for the time during the year that the employee was not a specified employee)25: 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365)

body.text: where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the tax year ends and B is the number of days in the tax year that the claimant employed the individual19. If a specified employee is employed by associated corporations (or entities deemed associated under Regulation 2900(10)), the combined salary included across all associated corporations cannot exceed 2.5 × A and must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T117424.
C. The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4))

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, salary, wages, or bonuses incurred as an SR&ED expense in a taxation year must actually be paid within 180 days following the end of that taxation year34. If an amount remains unpaid after 180 days, it is deducted on Line 315 of Form T661 and is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year; it can only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (and remains excluded from the proxy salary base under Regulation 2900(9))19.
D. Permissible Foreign SR&ED Salaries and Wages (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5))

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA, a claimant may include permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada (Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661), deemed to be an expenditure made in Canada and eligible for ITCs, only if four statutory conditions are met10: (1) the foreign SR&ED work is directly undertaken by employees of the claimant (never contractors); (2) the foreign work forms an integral part of, and is solely in support of, SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant; (3) the salary or wages paid for the foreign work are not subject to income or profits tax from a foreign country; and (4) the total permissible foreign SR&ED salary or wages claimed in the taxation year is capped at 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salary or wages paid for SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant in that year10.
3.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Supplies, and Experimental Production

Under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations (Traditional Method) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA (Proxy Method), a claimant may claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada19. As set out in the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy35:

"Materials for SR&ED" refer strictly to physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is being carried out, or that results from the SR&ED (including an intermediate product, by-product, or final product)35. Materials consumed (Line 320) occur when raw materials, substances, or items are destroyed, rendered useless, or used up in the prosecution of SR&ED (such as cardboard boxes and ink destroyed in printing tests, galvanized metal parts destroyed during testing, process water entering a chemical reaction and rendered valueless, or incremental feed/fertilizer in agricultural tests)19. Materials transformed (Line 325) occur when materials or component parts (such as an experimental engine placed in a machine) are physically incorporated into another product, intermediate product, custom product, or commercial asset as a result of the SR&ED process19.

The cost of materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (not when removed from inventory, manufactured without experimental development, or received from a supplier), and must be paid within 180 days of the tax year-end to earn an ITC in that year22. Cost is determined on a GAAP "laid-down cost" basis (including invoice cost, customs/excise duties, transportation, storage, acquisition costs, and third-party services such as galvanization required to bring a starting material into condition for SR&ED testing; for internally manufactured inventory, cost includes direct materials, direct labour, and a share of manufacturing overhead even under the proxy method)35. Under subsection 127(11.6), if materials are acquired from a non-arm's-length supplier, the ITC calculation is capped at the actual cost incurred by the supplier, excluding profit margins19.

Items that do not physically compose the body of the experimental object—such as office or lab supplies, utility water (e.g., washing floors), boiler feed water, and energy (electricity, gas, fuel) used to run equipment or heat labs/greenhouses—are not materials for SR&ED (under the Traditional Method, incremental utilities and supplies may be claimed as overhead on Line 360; energy qualifies as a material cost only if it physically enters and becomes part of the chemical/industrial conversion process)35. Finally, if items containing materials transformed or experimental production are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, ITC Recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) apply to recover the previously claimed tax credit1.
3.5 Subcontractors, Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 30, 2022) and Third-Party Payments Policy, external R&D expenditures are divided into three distinct legal categories28.
A. Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) — Line 340)

When a claimant contracts an arm's-length person or partnership to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada, 100% of the allowable contract expenditure is added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 340), but under subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, only 80% of the expenditure qualifies as a "qualified expenditure" for ITC purposes (a mandatory 20% reduction is applied on Line 529 of Form T661)19. Prepayments for SR&ED work not yet performed are barred by subsection 18(9)28.

To qualify on Form T661 and earn ITCs, the contracted SR&ED work must be performed in Canada by a taxable supplier22. If contracted SR&ED work is performed entirely outside Canada, no portion is allowable on Form T661 or for ITCs (though current expenditures for foreign research may be deducted in computing ordinary business income under subsection 37(2))28. If a contract is performed partially in Canada and partially outside Canada, only the reasonable portion allocated to SR&ED performed in Canada qualifies28. Under the former look-through rule in subsections 37(14) and 37(15) (repealed by Bill C-15, S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 5, as part of the restoration of capital expenditure eligibility), a payer's SR&ED contract expenditure had to be reduced by any related non-current expenditures of the performer, and the performer had to notify the payer in writing within 90 days after the end of the calendar year2. Furthermore, if an arm's-length contract expenditure remains unpaid 180 days after the tax year-end (subsection 127(26)), two reductions are recorded in Part 4 of Form T661: first, the 20% contract reduction; second, a reduction of the remaining 80% as an unpaid amount (with 80% added back in the subsequent year when paid, provided the unpaid amount was identified on time)22.
B. Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Contracts and Transfers (Subsections 127(11.6) & 127(13) — Line 345 & Form T1146)

When a claimant contracts a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer to perform SR&ED, the expenditure is entered on Line 345 for the Section 37 pool, but is completely deducted on Line 541 in Part 4 and does not directly earn an ITC for the payer19. Instead, the NAL performer either claims the ITCs itself or executes Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) to transfer its qualified SR&ED expenditures (including its PPA) from Line 540 of the performer's Form T661 to Line 508 of the payer's Form T6612. The performer cannot transfer more than its qualified SR&ED expenditure pool at year-end (if it attempts to do so, the Act states that no amount can be transferred), and partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures on Form T1146 because a partnership is not a "person" for these rules22.
C. Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii) & (iii) — Line 370 & Form T1263)

Unlike an SR&ED contract—where the payer controls the SR&ED work, holds exclusive rights to the results, and claims costs on an accrual basis—a third-party payment is a payment in cash or in kind (valued at fair market value) made to an approved entity (approved university, college, research institute, approved association, or granting council) or to a Canadian-resident corporation or tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation to be used for basic or applied SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business, where rights are non-exclusive (generally published) and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results28. Third-party payments are claimed on a cash basis when paid, require attaching a completed Form T1263 for each payment, are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool (Line 370), and are converted at 80% for ITC purposes (Line 529)19.
3.6 Overhead, Cloud Computing, Software Licensing, and Utilities

Under the Traditional Method, paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations permit claiming current overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 only if they pass a two-part statutory test set out in the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (and confirmed in Ergorecherche et Conseils Inc. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1710; Quantetics Corporation v. The Queen, 2000 DTC 2177; and Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877)23:

items: Directly Related Test: There must be a direct connection—without any intervening step or intermediary—between the expenditure and (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED, supported by rational and non-arbitrary allocation methods38.
Incremental Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred19.

body.text: In applying these rules to technology, facility, and administrative costs, the CRA's policies establish clear boundaries22:

items: Cloud Computing Infrastructure and Dedicated Bandwidth: Cloud computing infrastructure used specifically for experimental prototypes and testing is eligible when tracked in a separate expense bucket from commercial production infrastructure, whereas production cloud infrastructure is ineligible51. Furthermore, under the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 22, 2026), costs associated with bandwidth incurred after December 15, 2024, are explicitly allowed even under the Proxy Method as an equipment lease expenditure, provided the bandwidth is dedicated to SR&ED and is not general-purpose office equipment (GPOEF)27.

Telephone, Cellular, and General Internet: Fixed monthly payments for telephone, cell phone, or general office internet fail the incremental test because they would be incurred regardless of SR&ED; only specific, identifiable incremental charges (such as long-distance telephone charges directly for SR&ED) are allowed under the Traditional Method38.

Personnel Recruitment, Relocation, and Training (Traditional Method Only): Headhunter fees, job advertising, interview travel, and immigration/visa costs are disallowed as pre-employment ordinary business expenses lacking a direct link to SR&ED38. However, moving expenses to relocate selected candidates or hands-on SR&ED employees within Canada (subsection 62(3)), housing-loss taxable benefits (subsections 6(19)–(20)), and technical training costs for SR&ED are allowable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method (under the Proxy Method, all training and personnel costs are covered by the 55% PPA)19.

Prescribed Expenditures Excluded from ITCs (Regulation 2902): General administrative or management salaries not directed to SR&ED, legal and accounting fees, interest and financing costs, entertainment, advertising/selling expenses, conference/convention fees, membership dues, fines/penalties, and fees charged by claim preparers to prepare SR&ED claims are prescribed expenditures that never qualify for ITCs22.

body.text: 3.7 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Effective for depreciable property acquired (and becoming available for use for the first time) after December 15, 2024, and lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 restores the capital and lease expenditure eligibility that had been repealed from 2014 through December 15, 20242.
A. SR&ED Capital Expenditures: The 90% ASA Test (Paragraph 37(1)(b) & Subsection 127(9))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure made after December 15, 2024, to acquire depreciable property (property with an expected useful life exceeding 12 months on which CCA could be claimed under subsection 13(21)) qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure (claimed on Line 390 of Form T661) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that the property would either2:

items: Be used during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada (with non-SR&ED usage not exceeding 10%); OR
Have all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada2.

body.text: The property must become available for use for the first time after December 15, 2024 (subsection 37(1.2)), and its capital cost includes purchase price, installation costs, customs/excise duties, transportation, and direct acquisition costs (excluding borrowed money costs under section 21)2. Eligible SR&ED capital expenditures are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool (deemed to be CCA claimed) or carried forward indefinitely21.

Crucially, while both new and used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test can be included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (Line 390), used depreciable property is a prescribed expenditure under subparagraph 2902(b)(iii) of the Regulations (deducted on Line 535 of Form T661) and does NOT qualify for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITCs)2. Only new depreciable property earns the 35% or 15% SR&ED ITC, and for CCPCs and ECPCs within their $6.0 million expenditure limit, the 35% enhanced ITC earned on new capital expenditures is 40% refundable (14.0% effective cash refund)1. Land, leasehold interests in land, buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, inventory, and goodwill are strictly excluded under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e)2. Claimants must report on Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661 the names and SR&ED operating-time percentages of the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024, for each project2.
B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE): The >50% to <90% Primary-Use Regime (Subsection 127(9))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), if a claimant acquires new depreciable property after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA test, is not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for commercial plant commissioning or non-SR&ED over its useful life), it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods if it is actually used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada2:

items: First-Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): If used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED during the "first period" (from acquisition/available-for-use until the end of the first tax year ending at least 12 months after acquisition), 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost is deemed a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes2.

Second-Term SUE (Additional 25% of Capital Cost): If it qualified as First-Term SUE and is used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED during the "second period" (from acquisition until the end of the first tax year ending at least 24 months after acquisition), an additional 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost (50% cumulative) qualifies for ITCs2.

body.text: The capital cost of SUE is not included in the Section 37 pool and must be depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule 8 (T2SCH8) (where, for assets acquired on or after September 15, 2026, the proposed permanent Productivity Mega Deduction would permit up to a 100% first-year CCA write-off alongside the SUE ITC)2. If ASA capital property or SUE is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, ITC Recapture (subsections 127(27) to 127(36)) and CCA recapture rules apply1.
C. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Incurred After December 15, 2024)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 22, 2026), equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, qualify as current expenditures (earning 100% refundable ITCs at the 35% enhanced rate) as follows10:

body.text: 4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer corporate R&D tax credits6. Three jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit4. Except for Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through schedules filed with the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return4.
4.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
Ontario operates three distinct R&D tax credits codified under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and administered by the CRA6.

First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), enacted under Section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 and claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566) and Schedule T2SCH31, provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (10% for tax years ending before June 1, 2016) to corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations and prorated for short tax years), yielding a maximum annual refund of $240,0004. Ontario has not adopted the federal $6.0 million expenditure limit3. The $3,000,000 OITC limit phases out when prior-year federal taxable income of the associated group is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year specified paid-up / taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,0003. Official Government of Ontario guidance (updated October 30, 2026) confirms that OITC qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 20248.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), enacted under Sections 38 to 45 of the Taxation Act, 2007 and claimed on Schedule 508 (T2SCH508), provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure cap3. The eligible expenditure base for the ORDTC must first be reduced by the amount of any OITC and OBRITC claimed for the year8. Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, or formally waived in writing on or before 6 months after the tax year-end3.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), enacted under Section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007 and claimed on Schedule 568 (T2SCH568) and Schedule 569 (T2SCH569) (one Schedule 569 per contract), provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under eligible R&D contracts with Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs), capped at $20,000,000 in qualified contract expenditures annually across an associated group (up to $4,000,000 in refundable credits, prorated if the tax year is less than 51 weeks)4.
4.2 Quebec: The New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

In the Quebec Budget 2025–2026 and Quebec Budget 2026–2027, the Ministère des Finances du Québec enacted a comprehensive overhaul of Quebec's R&D tax incentives13. Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec replaced eight legacy tax measures—including the R&D Wage Credit (former Form RD-1029.7), the University Research Credit, the Pre-Competitive Private Partnership Credit, and the Industrial Design Credit (and abolished the Consortium Fee Credit, Technological Adaptation Credit, and Foreign Researcher/Expert Tax Holidays)—with the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC / Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation), codified under sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Taxation Act (Quebec) (alongside sections 222 to 230 for R&D deductions)8.

The CRIC is 100% refundable for all corporations regardless of size, asset value, or foreign control4. It provides an enhanced 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the annual exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable rate on all qualified expenditures above the $1,000,000 ceiling4. In addition to traditional R&D (where Quebec's definition is harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) and reviewed scientifically by the CRA), the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities undertaken in continuity with Quebec R&D work: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements for initial approval or certification; (2) product design (form, aesthetics, functionality improvements, and choice of materials); and (3) quality control activities related strictly to implementing a quality control system required for initial approval or certification3.

Qualified CRIC expenditures comprise 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors (including contracts with eligible public research centres, research consortia, CCTTs/CLTs, or university entities) for work carried out in Quebec, and 100% of capital property acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property claimed under the C3i credit)8. To qualify, annual expenditures must exceed an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount under the Quebec personal income tax system for each employee, adjusted in proportion to the time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities8. Claimants file separately with Revenu Québec (with their CO-17 return) using mandatory Form RD-222 and Form RD-1029.8.CR-T / RD-1029.8.CR (and RD-1029.8.PR where applicable)4.
4.3 British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

In British Columbia, under Sections 97 to 103 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), B.C. Budget 2026 made the 10% B.C. SR&ED Tax Credit permanent and expressly aligned B.C. with all principal federal Bill C-15 reforms for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 20243. Qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn a 10% refundable credit up to the expanded $6,000,000 expenditure limit (up to $600,000 cash back, phasing out over $15M–$75M prior-year taxable capital / revenue), while excess expenditures and non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward)3. Capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024, are restored as B.C. qualified expenditures, and claims are filed on Form T666 (Schedule 425 / T2SCH425) within 18 months of the tax year-end3.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act), administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA), operates independently of the federal $6.0M limit and retains a $4,000,000 annual eligible expenditure cap (phasing out between $10M and $50M of taxable capital)3. It provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's historical base level (average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 years) and a 20% refundable payment (8% base + 12% incremental) on spending above that two-year average, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the AT1 filing due date3.

In Saskatchewan (Sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000, claimed on Schedule 403 / T2SCH403), for qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, CCPCs earn a 10% refundable credit on their first $2,000,000 of annual qualifying expenditures (doubled from $1,000,000 previously; not extended to ECPCs)3. Expenditures above $2,000,000 and expenditures of non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward), subject to a $1,000,000 maximum combined annual credit cap3.

In Manitoba (Section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), claimed on Schedule 380 / T2SCH380 within 1 year after the filing due date), the province provides a 15% credit where 50% (7.5%) is refundable and 50% (7.5%) is non-refundable (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward) for in-house R&D, and 100% (15%) is refundable for R&D conducted under contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute (with 100% contract eligibility for Manitoba educational institutions)3. Manitoba never repealed capital expenditure eligibility in 2014, so depreciable R&D capital property (excluding buildings) has continuously qualified3.

Across the Atlantic Provinces and Yukon, New Brunswick (Section 59, New Brunswick Income Tax Act, Schedule 360 / T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (Section 41, Income Tax Act [NS], Schedule 340 / T2SCH340, 18-month deadline), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Section 42, Income Tax Act [NL], Schedule 301 / T2SCH301 or Form T1129, 12 months after filing due date) each provide a 15% fully refundable credit open to all corporations regardless of size or foreign control4. Uniquely, Newfoundland and Labrador eligible expenditures are not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits)6. Yukon (Section 15, Income Tax Act [Yukon], Schedule 442 / T2SCH442 or Form T1232, 18-month deadline) provides a 15% fully refundable credit plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University4.

body.text: 5. Interaction with Government Assistance, Grants (NRC IRAP), and Stacking Mechanics
5.1 Statutory Framework for Assistance and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, and as detailed in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (updated March 27, 2026), federal SR&ED tax incentives are provided strictly on the net out-of-pocket costs of performing SR&ED in Canada26. Both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Lines 429–432 of Form T661) and the Section 127 qualified SR&ED expenditure pool (Lines 513–517 of Form T661) must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance (inducements or reimbursements included under paragraph 12(1)(x)), or (for ITC purposes) contract payments that the claimant "has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive" on or before the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year19. Reductions are calculated on a project-by-project basis and cannot reduce a project's SR&ED expenditures below zero (nil)26.

Under subsection 127(9), "government assistance" means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and indirect government funding delivered through non-profit organizations)—whether provided as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—other than the federal SR&ED ITC26. Consequently, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (e.g., Ontario OITC/ORDTC/OBRITC, Quebec CRIC, B.C. SR&ED credit, Alberta IEG, Nova Scotia 15% credit) as well as direct R&D grants such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) (which cost-shares R&D salaries and contractor costs, often covering up to 80% of eligible R&D labour) reduce the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool in the taxation year the expenditures are incurred4. Furthermore, if a loan agreement contains repayment conditions dependent on future success or revenues (e.g., repayable only upon reaching a specified sales or profit threshold), the CRA treats the funding as a forgivable loan (assistance) rather than an ordinary business loan, reducing the SR&ED pool immediately until such time as any repayment is actually made20.

6. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Audit Administration
6.1 Institutional Governance and Program Scale

Canada's federal R&D tax incentive system is governed jointly by the Department of Finance Canada (which sets statutory tax policy, credit rates, and legislative amendments) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (which administers technical and financial reviews and processes claims through its SR&ED Directorate and regional coordinating tax services offices in Surrey, B.C.; Toronto, Ontario; Laval, Quebec; and Halifax, Nova Scotia)9. According to official CRA program statistics, during Fiscal Year 2024–2025 the SR&ED program delivered $4.5 billion in ITCs to more than 19,000 claimants across over 22,000 processed claims; for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, the CRA reported $4.9 billion in ITCs claimed and $4.6 billion allowed, representing roughly a 50% climb in credit value since fiscal 20229. In the most recent reporting year, roughly 96% of SR&ED claims resulted in credits—with 90% accepted as filed, 6% accepted after modifications, and 4% denied9.
