body.text: 6.3 The Statutory 18-Month Reporting Deadline

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, the SR&ED reporting deadline to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the year in which the expenditure was incurred18. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing due date is 6 months after the end of its tax year, a corporation's SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 18 months after the end of its tax year (for individuals, whose T1 return is due June 15, the reporting deadline is June 15 of the following year, or 17.5 months after a December 31 year-end)9.

Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12), late filings are not accepted under any circumstances: if Form T661 is not filed with the prescribed information by the 18-month reporting deadline, the expenditures are deemed not to be SR&ED expenditures, forfeiting both the Section 37 pool deduction and all Section 127 ITCs18. If Form T661 is filed on time by the 18-month deadline but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the 18-month deadline, the claimant may still deduct the allowable expenditures in the Section 37 pool, but permanently loses all entitlement to ITCs on those expenditures18.
6.4 The April 1, 2026 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process, Review Standards, and Objections

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (supported by the SR&ED Client Portal Pre-Claim Workbook inside My Business Account and the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool [SALT])2. Businesses can submit a technical project summary and cost estimate for CRA evaluation prior to filing their full return11. Whereas the standard CRA service standard for refundable claims selected for review is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (non-refundable claims have no service standard), claims granted pre-claim approval that require only an expenditure review are processed within 90 calendar days—cutting review processing times in half (unless the project changed significantly from the pre-approved scope or unapproved projects are included, in which case the 180-day standard applies)9.

As detailed in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), once a claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn because Form T661 certification cannot be revoked11. Technical eligibility is reviewed by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and financial allowability is audited by a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM])11. Under judicial precedent cited in the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, the CRA has authority to expand the scope of a review to additional projects or issues as facts emerge (Ludmer / Ludco Enterprises Ltd. v. MNR, 93 DTC 1351), and the relevance of documents requested by an RTA is broadly construed (The Queen v. McKinley Transport Ltd., 90 DTC 6243; AGT Ltd. v. Canada, 97 DTC 5189)65. If adjustments or penalties are proposed, the CRA issues a draft SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and a Proposal Letter, providing the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations11. Unresolved procedural or policy concerns can be escalated to the RTM/FRM for an Administrative Second Review, and following the issuance of a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant has 90 calendar days to file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, followed by a statutory right of appeal to the Tax Court of Canada11.
7. Judicial Precedents, Case Law Analysis, and Evidentiary Standards
7.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants and C.W. Agencies

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), Chief Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada established the five-question common-law test for determining whether activities constitute SR&ED under subsection 248(1), which was adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (affirming 2000 DTC 2372 (TCC))7:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? ("Routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; if resolution is reasonably predictable using standard procedures, no technological uncertainty exists)7.
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?7
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of the hypotheses?7
Did the process result in a technological advancement? (Which includes an advancement in general understanding, even if an experiment rejects a hypothesis)7.
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?7

body.text: In C.W. Agencies Inc. (2000 DTC 2372 (TCC); 2001 FCA 393), the courts applied this standard to software and information systems, holding that routine activities such as defining requirements, evaluating commercial products, testing hardware configurations, or routine software testing are conducted by "competent and prudent users of complex, commercially available technologies," whereas eligible computer science SR&ED requires systematic investigation to discover new knowledge, concepts, principles, technologies, or techniques65.
7.2 Evidentiary Standards: Contemporaneous Documentation, Oral Testimony, and Cost Constraints
Canadian jurisprudence has clarified both the legal status of contemporaneous documentation and the role of economic/contextual constraints:

items: 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, [1998] A.C.I. No. 478 (TCC) and Abeilles Inc. v. The Queen (TCC, October 2014): In 116736 Canada Inc., Justice Archambault explained—and Justice Jorré reaffirmed in Abeilles—that while a taxpayer attempting to convince the Minister or the Tax Court without contemporary written test reports puts itself in a "very precarious position," the Income Tax Act and Regulations do not require written contemporaneous reports as a mandatory legal condition for SR&ED recognition; a taxpayer may adduce evidence via credible oral testimony68. Moreover, in Abeilles, the Tax Court held that the need to develop a cost-effective solution can constitute genuine technological uncertainty where existing technical solutions cannot achieve the required performance within severe cost or physical constraints33.

Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 159: In allowing a food-science SR&ED appeal involving the development of a cold-pressed, vinegar-based drink shelf-stable at room temperature, Justice Bodie established two key principles7: (1) a scientific or technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution or preservative exists, provided it has never been used in the specific context and the taxpayer proves on a balance of probabilities that the uncertainty could not be resolved through routine engineering7; and (2) contemporaneous documentation is meant simply to keep track of the hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained as work progresses—it does not need to be designed for someone unfamiliar with the field of science or technology to replicate the results70.

body.text: 7.3 The Objective Standard of the "Competent Professional" and Expert Witness Admissibility
Recent Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal decisions from 2017 through 2026 highlight three strict audit and litigation principles:

First, technological uncertainty is an objective standard measured against a "competent professional" in the relevant domain, not the subjective knowledge of the taxpayer67. The Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal dismissed taxpayer appeals in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6, where the taxpayer called no engineers or scientists to establish what standard rigging techniques were accessible to mechanical engineers)67; Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88, affirming TCC October 2019, confirming that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the binding legal interpretation of s. 248(1) and holding that routine technical issues in stamping parts with different materials do not constitute technological uncertainty)42; Logic Data Products Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC, holding that uncertainty does not exist simply because the taxpayer lacks knowledge in solar shingles)67; Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen (2022 TCC, rejecting the subjective view of four non-engineers/non-mechanics taking apart a fuel injector)67; JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC, where a welding specialist offered no expert evidence from electrical or network engineers regarding sensor noise and network integration)67; and Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC, decided September 2025, holding that product novelty alone does not establish technological uncertainty and that the appellant must prove an objective gap in existing scientific or technological knowledge)67.

Second, expert witnesses must be strictly independent and must not usurp the court's role42. In National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72, affirming 2020 TCC 47), the Federal Court of Appeal held that the CRA's 2021 SR&ED guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method and upheld the exclusion of the taxpayer's expert report under the White Burgess standard because the taxpayer had written the majority of the report (making it an "exercise in advocacy") and the report impermissibly opined on how the law applied to the facts42. (Similarly, in Abeilles, Justice Jorré discounted the testimony of a CRA scientific adviser who confused his audit role with that of an expert witness by relying on CRA policies rather than independent personal expertise68.) Conversely, in Allegro Wireless Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 27) and Abeilles (TCC, October 2014), taxpayers won their appeals by calling truly independent, qualified experts who testified authoritatively to the scientific method and technological advancements achieved42. In dTechs EPM Ltd. v. British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority (2023 FCA 115; 2026 FC 1235, decided October 6, 2026), the Federal Court of Appeal and Federal Court further clarified that while counsel may facilitate report preparation by recording an expert's answers during videoconferences, the substantive opinions must genuinely remain the independent work of the expert74.

Third, statutory filing deadlines are strictly enforced. In Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. (2016, FCA Docket A-432-15), even though the Minister accepted that the appellant had incurred valid SR&ED expenditures for deduction purposes, the Court upheld the complete denial of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit because the taxpayer failed to file prescribed Form T661 containing the prescribed information by the statutory deadline78.
